strengths: Provides a rigorous, exact geometric characterization (feasible PPV/FOR region, star-convexity, piecewise hyperbolic boundary) of classifiers attainable from a group-calibrated score, extending prior work (Baumann et al., 2022) that required continuity and full-support assumptions to the practically relevant finite-valued score setting.

Derives a clean and efficient post-processing algorithm (boundary tracing via the fractional-knapsack-style greedy rule) that computes the optimal sufficiency-constrained classifier for a broad class of loss functions, with explicit closed-form reduction to solving quadratics.

Extends the analysis to a second, practically important objective—minimizing deviation from separation subject to sufficiency—showing it can be optimized within the same geometric/algorithmic framework, which nicely bridges two fairness notions known to be generally incompatible.

The paper is well organized theoretically, connects clearly to established fairness literature (Chouldechova, Kleinberg et al., Hardt et al., Canetti et al., Baumann et al., Benger & Ligett), and includes detailed proofs for essentially all claims in the appendix.
The COMPAS case study offers a concrete, interpretable illustration of the method, showing group-specific threshold behavior and near-optimal accuracy relative to the unconstrained optimum.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is minimal: only a single dataset (COMPAS) and a single illustrative run are reported, without comparison to alternative approaches for achieving sufficiency (e.g., Canetti et al.'s abstention-based method or Baumann et al.'s post-processing), and without any assessment of variability/robustness across data splits or datasets.

The entire framework assumes the population distribution P(Y,S,A) (and thus perfect group-calibration) is known exactly; finite-sample estimation error in calibration curves and score distributions is not analyzed, even though the COMPAS experiment relies on empirically estimated calibration curves from a data split, which could materially affect the correctness/robustness of the derived optimal classifier in practice.

The method may require randomized decisions at breakpoints, which raises practical and ethical considerations (e.g., transparency, reproducibility, and acceptability of randomized decisions in high-stakes settings such as bail) that are not discussed.

The main text focuses exclusively on the binary-group case; while the authors state the extension to multiple groups is straightforward, this is not demonstrated, and the combinatorial complexity of tracing pairwise boundaries for more than two groups is left unaddressed.

Limited discussion of how sensitive the practical usefulness of the approach is to violations of the group-calibration assumption (the paper notes COMPAS scores are not properly calibrated and relies on an ad hoc recalibration procedure, but does not quantify how deviations from true calibration affect the guarantees).

strengths: Provides a rigorous, exact geometric characterization (star-convexity, piecewise hyperbolic boundary structure) of the feasible PPV/FOR region for binary classifiers built on calibrated scores, which is a genuinely novel and elegant analytical tool.

Extends prior work (Baumann et al., 2022) that assumed continuous, full-support score distributions to the practically important finite-valued score setting, which matches real systems like COMPAS and FICO that use discrete score bins.

Derives a concrete, efficient post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) that traces the boundary of the intersection of group-wise feasible regions and can optimize a wide class of objectives, including 0-1 loss and a deviation-from-separation measure, unifying two seemingly separate fairness problems within one framework.

Includes a formal robustness analysis bounding predictive-parity violation by twice the maximum calibration error when scores are only approximately group-calibrated, with both synthetic and real (ACS Income) empirical support, which strengthens practical applicability.

Empirical illustrations span three different real/semi-real datasets (FICO, COMPAS, ACS Income) with an end-to-end pipeline (including model training and calibration) for the ACS case, giving a reasonably complete picture of the method's applicability and reproducibility.

The observation and proof that classifiers minimizing deviation from separation can be found via the same boundary-tracing algorithm and often achieve near-optimal accuracy is a useful and non-obvious practical takeaway.
weaknesses: The framework and detailed algorithm are developed only for the binary-group case; extension to more than two protected groups is deferred entirely to future work, even though the conclusion acknowledges this is a significant practical limitation (feasibility becomes increasingly restrictive with more groups).

The method's central assumption of access to (exactly or approximately) group-calibrated finite-valued scores is fairly strong; in the COMPAS experiment, calibration is not verified but essentially constructed synthetically by assigning pooled empirical outcome rates to decile scores, which weakens the realism of that case study.

There is no empirical comparison against existing post-processing baselines for sufficiency/predictive parity (e.g., Baumann et al. 2022's continuous-score approach adapted to discretized data, or Zeng et al. 2022), making it hard to gauge practical advantages beyond the theoretical guarantees.

The deviation-from-separation analysis is tied to one specific total-variation-based measure (Benger & Ligett, 2025); it is unclear how sensitive the resulting optimal classifier and its favorable comparison to the loss-optimal one are to the choice of separation-deviation metric.

The presentation is very notation-heavy and mathematically dense (extensive appendices with many auxiliary lemmas), which may limit accessibility to a broader ICML audience despite the work's technical soundness.

The practical significance of exact sufficiency in real deployments is not deeply discussed—since exact predictive parity is a stringent binary-decision fairness notion, and the paper does not discuss when practitioners would prefer this exact approach over approximate or relaxed alternatives beyond a brief mention in the conclusion.
